sentences.back: Setting up a home compost system is a great step toward sustainability and reducing waste, especially for anyone interested in gardening.
This do-it-yourself project lets you turn kitchen scraps and yard trimmings into rich organic matter that nourishes your plants.
The basic principle behind composting is simple: microorganisms break down organic matter.
To promote this process effectively, you need to give them the right conditions.
Good compost bins can be bought, and you can also easily make one yourself from a few planks or even old pallets.
The ideal spot for a compost bin gets some sun but is not completely exposed to bad weather.
It should also be convenient for adding materials and turning the compost.
Balancing 'greens' and 'browns' in the compost pile is the key to success.
'Greens' are nitrogen-rich materials, such as fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds and grass clippings.
'Browns' are carbon-rich materials, such as dry leaves, shredded newspaper and cardboard.
A rough rule of thumb is that the ratio of browns to greens is about two to one.
Too many greens turn into a wet, smelly mess, while too many browns slow decomposition down greatly.
When adding kitchen scraps, avoid meat, dairy or greasy food, because these attract pests and produce bad smells.
Grass clippings should be added in thin layers to keep them from clumping together and becoming starved of oxygen.
It is also a good idea to cut larger items into smaller pieces.
This increases the surface area for microbes to work on and speeds up decomposition.
Turning your compost pile regularly is another key aspect.
This process, often called aeration, brings oxygen into the pile, and oxygen is essential for the aerobic bacteria that do most of the decomposing.
Try to turn it every one to two weeks.
You know the compost is ready when it has a dark, crumbly texture and smells earthy, much like a forest floor after rain.

The finished compost can then be spread around your garden beds, improving soil structure and giving your plants important nutrients, thereby closing the loop on your waste-reduction efforts in a truly organic way and boosting your garden's yield.
It is a rewarding do-it-yourself undertaking that, by promoting sustainability, benefits both your garden and the planet.
